record.paper_title: Cyber-Physical Attacks on UAS Networks–Challenges and Open Research Problems
record.context_brief: Security analysis of UAS routing mechanisms
record.original_question: How secure are proposed routing mechanisms for flying ad hoc or UAS networks that calculate paths in rapidly changing topologies under stringent latency constraints, and how should those methods be technically analyzed and compared for security-specific vulnerabilities rather than relying on inherited assumptions from MANET routing?

evidence.quote: The highly dynamic nature of UAS networks, as well as stringent requirements on latency, necessitate novel routing mechanisms capable of calculating paths in rapidly changing topologies. A survey of the state of the art in this area is presented in [14]. The proposed methods may be prone to potential vulnerabilities, and the demand for a detailed technical analysis and comparison of these proposals in terms of their security is yet to be fulfilled.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the class of routing protocols designed for flying ad hoc networks (FANETs) and unmanned aerial system (UAS) networks, in which a set of mobile aerial nodes must establish and maintain multi-hop communication paths under (i) rapidly changing network topologies caused by high node mobility and frequent link breakages, and (ii) stringent end-to-end latency constraints on path computation and packet delivery. Many such protocols are adapted from, or inherit assumptions of, mobile ad hoc network (MANET) routing protocols (e.g., reactive, proactive, geographic, position-based, hierarchical, and cluster-based schemes).

Develop a rigorous technical framework that:

1. Defines a formal adversary model appropriate to UAS routing, specifying adversary capabilities (eavesdropping, packet injection, dropping, modification, replay, Sybil/identity spoofing, wormhole and sinkhole formation, rushing, blackhole/grayhole behavior, and compromise of legitimate nodes), adversary placement (internal vs. external), and computational/mobility resources.

2. Specifies a set of security properties that a UAS routing protocol must satisfy, including but not limited to: authenticity and integrity of routing control messages, freshness, resistance to topology disruption, route truthfulness, availability under adversarial churn, and bounded latency under attack.

3. Provides a methodology for analyzing each candidate UAS routing protocol against this adversary model — covering both formal/symbolic analysis of routing logic and quantitative analysis (under realistic mobility models and latency budgets) — that does not merely import security arguments from the MANET setting but explicitly accounts for the high-mobility, low-latency, three-dimensional, and energy-constrained characteristics of UAS networks.

4. Produces a comparative evaluation of existing UAS/FANET routing proposals using this framework, identifying for each protocol the specific vulnerabilities introduced or amplified by the UAS setting (as opposed to those already known from MANET analyses), and characterizing the trade-offs between security guarantees and the latency/topology-update requirements of UAS operation.

The problem is to construct such a framework and carry out the corresponding security analysis and comparison.
artifact.status_search_result: Surveys and research on FANET/UAS routing security through 2024–2025 continue to identify the lack of a unified, UAS-specific security analysis framework for routing protocols and emphasize that most evaluations still inherit MANET assumptions. No single work appears to have delivered a comprehensive comparative security analysis of proposed UAS routing mechanisms tailored to high-mobility, low-latency settings, so the question remains open.
